warmup.q: Three workers each run SELECT job_id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'queued' ORDER BY run_after LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE and keep their transaction open while the job runs, 2 seconds. Five jobs are queued. What happens?
options: They get three different jobs at once: FOR UPDATE makes each worker lock a different row
Worker 1 gets the oldest job; workers 2 and 3 wait for it, and each moves to the next job only after the worker ahead of it commits
All three get the oldest job, and the job runs three times
Workers 2 and 3 fail at once with a lock error
warmup.why: All three pick the same oldest row from the same snapshot, so two of them wait for the first one's lock. When it commits, PostgreSQL rechecks the row, finds it no longer queued and moves each waiter on to the next row, where they collide again. No job runs twice, but the workers run one at a time. Three different jobs at once is what SKIP LOCKED gives you; an immediate error is NOWAIT.

sections.h: Two workers that read the queue run the same job twice
sections.html:
The jobs table is a to-do list for background work: send a receipt, settle a merchant's day, review a payment for fraud. In the seed, five of its eight rows are queued and due, and the oldest is job 2, a fraud review of payment 31. A worker is a loop: find the oldest due job, mark it running, do the work, mark it done. You run three workers so that three jobs run at once.

The first version of the claim is a read, then a write:

SELECT job_id FROM jobs
WHERE status = 'queued' AND run_after <= now()
ORDER BY run_after, job_id LIMIT 1;                         -- 2
UPDATE jobs SET status = 'running', locked_by = 'worker-a', attempts = attempts + 1
WHERE job_id = 2;

Two workers that start a few milliseconds apart both read job 2, because neither has written yet. Both update it. The second UPDATE waits until the first one commits, then writes over it. Job 2 ends with attempts = 2 and locked_by = 'worker-b', and the fraud team reviews payment 31 twice. For a receipt job, the customer gets two emails. It is the lost update of lesson 12 ("Transactions and isolation levels") with a job instead of a balance.

The wait in the middle is the useful part. An UPDATE marks each row it changes as taken by its transaction until that transaction ends. That mark is a row lock: anyone else who wants to change the row, or lock it, waits for COMMIT or ROLLBACK. A plain SELECT never waits for it; it reads the last committed version and walks past. PostgreSQL writes the mark into the row itself, in the header of the row version on its 8 KB page, so a million locked rows cost no memory, only page writes. A transaction that has to wait sleeps on the holder's transaction id in the server's lock manager and wakes when that transaction ends. The database internals track builds this machinery in "Concurrency control: locks, deadlocks and SSI".

SELECT ... FOR UPDATE takes the same lock at read time, so reading and claiming become one step:

SELECT job_id FROM jobs
WHERE status = 'queued' AND run_after <= now()
ORDER BY run_after, job_id LIMIT 1
FOR UPDATE;

Now the second worker's SELECT waits on job 2. When the first worker commits, PostgreSQL checks job 2 against the WHERE clause again, sees running, drops it, and returns job 3. No job runs twice. But the second worker sat idle until the first one committed, and a worker that keeps its transaction open while it works commits only when its job is done. With 2-second fraud reviews, three workers finish one job every 2 seconds: the speed of one. In Kotlin terms, FOR UPDATE is synchronized on the row, and all three workers want the same row.

try.title: Two workers, one job
steps: Open two terminals in the labs folder and run psql in both: docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz -d course. Call them A and B. Start the database if it is not running (docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait, from the labs folder).
In B, run \timing on so psql prints how long each statement took. Then run the first block, switching terminals at each comment. B's UPDATE hangs until A commits.
Before the SELECT at the end, predict attempts and locked_by for job 2. Then run the FOR UPDATE block the same way: which job does B's SELECT return, and when?

code.title: psql, two sessions on database course
code.html: -- A BEGIN; SELECT job_id, kind FROM jobs WHERE status = 'queued' AND run_after <= now() ORDER BY run_after, job_id LIMIT 1; -- B BEGIN; SELECT job_id, kind FROM jobs WHERE status = 'queued' AND run_after <= now() ORDER BY run_after, job_id LIMIT 1; -- A: claim the job it read UPDATE jobs SET status = 'running', locked_by = 'worker-a', attempts = attempts + 1 WHERE job_id = 2; -- B: claim the job it read (this one waits) UPDATE jobs SET status = 'running', locked_by = 'worker-b', attempts = attempts + 1 WHERE job_id = 2; -- A COMMIT; -- B COMMIT; SELECT job_id, status, locked_by, attempts FROM jobs WHERE job_id = 2; UPDATE jobs SET status = 'queued', locked_by = NULL, locked_at = NULL, attempts = 0 WHERE job_id IN (2, 3); -- the same claim with FOR UPDATE: A, then B (it waits), then A's UPDATE and COMMIT BEGIN; -- A SELECT job_id, kind FROM jobs WHERE status = 'queued' AND run_after <= now() ORDER BY run_after, job_id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE; -- A BEGIN; -- B SELECT job_id, kind FROM jobs WHERE status = 'queued' AND run_after <= now() ORDER BY run_after, job_id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE; -- B (waits) UPDATE jobs SET status = 'running', locked_by = 'worker-a', attempts = attempts + 1 WHERE job_id = 2; -- A COMMIT; -- A ROLLBACK; -- B UPDATE jobs SET status = 'queued', locked_by = NULL, locked_at = NULL, attempts = 0 WHERE job_id IN (2, 3); -- put them back

try.expect:
Both SELECTs return job 2, fraud_review. B's UPDATE prints nothing until A's COMMIT, then (B, trimmed; your times will differ):

UPDATE 1
Time: 2328.650 ms (00:02.329)

 job_id | status  | locked_by | attempts
--------+---------+-----------+----------
      2 | running | worker-b  |        2
(1 row)

Two claims of one job, and no error anywhere: B waited for A's row lock and then overwrote A's claim. In the FOR UPDATE block, B's SELECT waits too, for as long as A keeps its transaction open, and then returns a different job:

 job_id |     kind
--------+--------------
      3 | send_receipt
(1 row)

Time: 2707.236 ms (00:02.707)

PostgreSQL rechecked job 2 after A committed, found it running, and moved on to job 3. Correct, but B was idle the whole time. The last statement puts both jobs back.

sections.h: SKIP LOCKED lets each worker take the next job nobody holds
sections.html:
The workers do not need job 2. Any due job will do. SKIP LOCKED says exactly that: when a row is locked by another transaction, skip it instead of waiting. The claim becomes one statement that picks, locks and marks a job, and returns it:

UPDATE jobs
SET status = 'running', locked_by = current_setting('application_name'),
    locked_at = now(), attempts = attempts + 1
WHERE job_id = (SELECT job_id FROM jobs
                WHERE status = 'queued' AND run_after <= now()
                ORDER BY run_after, job_id LIMIT 1
                FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)
RETURNING job_id, kind, payload;

Worker 1's subquery locks job 2. Worker 2's subquery finds job 2 locked, skips it, and locks job 3. Worker 3 skips 2 and 3 and locks 5. Each claim returns at once, and nobody waits. The outer UPDATE then changes a row its own subquery already holds, so it cannot wait either. LIMIT 1 keeps the lock to one row: PostgreSQL stops locking once the LIMIT has its rows. And the partial index jobs_ready_idx (on run_after, for queued rows only) keeps the search short however many done jobs pile up. The stepper below runs both versions with three workers.

There is a third option between waiting and skipping. NOWAIT makes the statement fail at once, with SQLSTATE 55P03 (could not obtain lock on row), when a row it wants is locked. Use it where a user should hear "this refund is being processed" rather than watch a spinner. The three map onto ReentrantLock in Kotlin: FOR UPDATE is lock(), NOWAIT is a tryLock() that throws, and SKIP LOCKED is tryLock() on each candidate in turn until one succeeds.

Once a worker has its job, it has to decide how long to hold it.

  1. Keep the transaction open while the job runs. The lock is the lease. If the worker's pod dies, its connection closes, PostgreSQL rolls the transaction back, and the job is queued again with nothing to clean up. The cost is one connection and one open transaction per running job. An open transaction also stops VACUUM from removing dead rows anywhere in the database (lesson 12).
  2. Claim and commit. The claim is its own short transaction; the work runs outside any transaction; a second short transaction marks the job done. Nothing is held while the work runs. But a crashed worker now leaves its job running forever, so a reaper must put back jobs whose locked_at is too old, counting attempts and giving up after a few (job 6 in the seed is failed after 3). A reaped job may already have half run, so the work must be safe to repeat.

Hold the lock for jobs that take a fraction of a second. Claim and commit for anything that calls a card issuer, an email provider or another service.

stepper.title: Three workers claim jobs: FOR UPDATE, SKIP LOCKED, NOWAIT
stepper.intro: Click Next. Each worker holds its transaction open while its job runs, about 2 seconds.

try.title: Three workers, no waiting
steps: Open three terminals in the labs folder and run psql in each: docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz -d course. Call them A, B and C. Start the database if it is not running (docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait, from the labs folder).

Name each worker and turn on timing: SET application_name = 'worker-1'; and \timing on in A, the same with 'worker-2' in B and 'worker-3' in C. The claim reads that name with current_setting('application_name').

Run BEGIN; and the claim in A, then B, then C, without committing. Which job does each get, and does any of them wait? Then run the rest of the block: a NOWAIT probe in B, a crash of C (its ROLLBACK), and a new claim in A.

code.title: psql, three sessions on database course
code.html: -- A, then B, then C: the same two statements BEGIN; UPDATE jobs SET status = 'running', locked_by = current_setting('application_name'), locked_at = now(), attempts = attempts + 1 WHERE job_id = (SELECT job_id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'queued' AND run_after <= now() ORDER BY run_after, job_id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) RETURNING job_id, kind, locked_by; -- A: is anybody waiting? SELECT application_name, state, wait_event_type FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE application_name LIKE 'worker-%' ORDER BY 1; -- B: the oldest queued job, but fail instead of waiting SELECT job_id, kind FROM jobs WHERE status = 'queued' ORDER BY run_after, job_id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE NOWAIT; \echo :SQLSTATE ROLLBACK; -- C: the worker crashes ROLLBACK; -- A: finish job 2, then claim again COMMIT; BEGIN; UPDATE jobs SET status = 'running', locked_by = current_setting('application_name'), locked_at = now(), attempts = attempts + 1 WHERE job_id = (SELECT job_id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'queued' AND run_after <= now() ORDER BY run_after, job_id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) RETURNING job_id, kind, locked_by; ROLLBACK; UPDATE jobs SET status = 'queued', locked_by = NULL, locked_at = NULL, attempts = 0 WHERE job_id IN (2, 3, 5);

try.expect:
Each claim returns at once with a different job (output trimmed; the times are a few milliseconds to a couple of hundred on a busy laptop):

-- A
 job_id |     kind     | locked_by
--------+--------------+-----------
      2 | fraud_review | worker-1
-- B
      3 | send_receipt | worker-2
-- C
      5 | settle_merchant | worker-3

pg_stat_activity shows nobody waiting: worker-1 is active (it is running that query), the other two are idle in transaction, and none has wait_event_type = Lock. B's NOWAIT probe fails at once with ERROR: could not obtain lock on row in relation "jobs" and 55P03, because job 2 is still queued in B's snapshot but locked by A. After C's ROLLBACK and A's COMMIT, A's new claim returns job 3: B's earlier ROLLBACK put job 3 back, and job 5, freed by C, is next in line. The last statement resets the three jobs.

sections.h: Four lock strengths, and why a payment insert locks its card
sections.html:
Here is a stranger wait. A support tool runs SELECT ... FROM cards WHERE card_id = 5 FOR UPDATE while an agent looks at Daniel's card. At the same moment a payment on card 5 arrives, and its INSERT into payments hangs until the agent's transaction ends. Nothing locked payments. Why does an insert wait for a lock on cards?

Because payments.card_id is a foreign key. The INSERT must make sure card 5 exists and keeps existing until the payment commits. If the agent's transaction deleted card 5 in the meantime, the payment would point at nothing. So the foreign-key check locks the card row, in the weakest mode there is. PostgreSQL has four row lock modes, strongest first:

  • FOR UPDATE is taken by DELETE, by an UPDATE that changes a key column (one with a unique index a foreign key could point at), and by SELECT ... FOR UPDATE.
  • FOR NO KEY UPDATE is taken by every other UPDATE, and by SELECT ... FOR NO KEY UPDATE.
  • FOR SHARE lets any number of transactions hold the row at once and blocks any UPDATE or DELETE of it by other transactions.
  • FOR KEY SHARE blocks only a DELETE or a change of the key. A foreign-key check takes this one on the parent row.

Which pairs conflict (X means the second one waits):

requested \ held KEY SHARE SHARE NO KEY UPDATE UPDATE
FOR KEY SHARE X
FOR SHARE X X
FOR NO KEY UPDATE X X X
FOR UPDATE X X X X

The foreign-key check's KEY SHARE conflicts only with FOR UPDATE. An ordinary UPDATE cards SET status = 'blocked' WHERE card_id = 5 takes NO KEY UPDATE, so payments on card 5 go through while it runs. The support tool's explicit FOR UPDATE claimed more than it needed: it will never delete the card or change its card_id. Lock with FOR NO KEY UPDATE when you lock a row to change its ordinary columns, and parent rows stop blocking their children. This split arrived in PostgreSQL 9.3; before it, foreign-key checks took SHARE locks and blocked every UPDATE of the parent.

try.title: Watch a foreign key take a lock
steps: Open three terminals in the labs folder and run psql in each: docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz -d course. Call them A, B and C. C only watches. Start the database if it is not running (docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait, from the labs folder).
In C, run CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pgrowlocks; once. Its function pgrowlocks('cards') reads the lock marks out of the table's rows.
Run the block, switching terminals at each comment. In the first round, B's INSERT hangs: look at C's output to see who it waits for. Predict the second and third rounds before you run them.

code.title: psql, three sessions on database course
code.html: -- round 1. A: lock card 5 the strong way BEGIN; SELECT card_id, status FROM cards WHERE card_id = 5 FOR UPDATE; -- B: a payment on card 5 (waits) BEGIN; INSERT INTO payments (card_id, merchant_id, amount_minor, status, created_at) VALUES (5, 2, 1500, 'pending', now()); -- C: who waits for whom, and what is on the row SELECT pid, wait_event_type, wait_event, pg_blocking_pids(pid) AS blocked_by, left(query, 40) AS query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE wait_event_type = 'Lock'; SELECT locked_row, locker, multi, modes, pids FROM pgrowlocks('cards'); -- A, then B ROLLBACK; ROLLBACK; -- round 2. A: lock it for an update of ordinary columns only BEGIN; SELECT card_id, status FROM cards WHERE card_id = 5 FOR NO KEY UPDATE; -- B: the same payment BEGIN; INSERT INTO payments (card_id, merchant_id, amount_minor, status, created_at) VALUES (5, 2, 1500, 'pending', now()); -- C SELECT locked_row, locker, multi, modes, pids FROM pgrowlocks('cards'); -- B ROLLBACK; -- round 3. A: a real UPDATE of the card, then B's payment once more, then C UPDATE cards SET status = 'blocked' WHERE card_id = 5; BEGIN; -- B INSERT INTO payments (card_id, merchant_id, amount_minor, status, created_at) VALUES (5, 2, 1500, 'pending', now()); -- B SELECT locked_row, locker, multi, modes, pids FROM pgrowlocks('cards'); -- C ROLLBACK; -- B ROLLBACK; -- A

try.expect:
In round 1, B's INSERT hangs and C shows why (your pids and transaction ids differ):

 pid | wait_event_type |  wait_event   | blocked_by |                  query
-----+-----------------+---------------+------------+------------------------------------------
 511 | Lock            | transactionid | {496}      | INSERT INTO payments (card_id, merchant_
(1 row)

 locked_row | locker | multi |     modes      | pids
------------+--------+-------+----------------+-------
 (0,5)      |    889 | f     | {"For Update"} | {496}
(1 row)

B waits on A's transaction id, not on the row: that is how a row lock wait looks from the outside. The lock itself sits on card 5's row version at page 0, slot 5. The moment A rolls back, B's INSERT finishes with INSERT 0 1. In round 2 B's INSERT returns at once, and the row carries two locks from two transactions, a MultiXact (multi = t):

 locked_row | locker | multi |                 modes                 |   pids
------------+--------+-------+---------------------------------------+-----------
 (0,5)      |      1 | t     | {"For No Key Update","For Key Share"} | {496,511}
(1 row)

For Key Share is the foreign-key check of B's INSERT. In round 3 A's real UPDATE adds No Key Update to the list, and B still does not wait. Every round ends in ROLLBACK, so nothing changes.

sections.h: Deadlocks come from taking locks in opposite orders
sections.html:
Ivy moves 1,000 from account 109 to 209 while a scheduled sweep moves 3,000 from 209 to 109. Each transfer is two UPDATEs, a debit and then a credit, and each UPDATE locks its row. Transfer A locks 109. Transfer B locks 209. A's credit needs 209, so A waits for B. B's credit needs 109, so B waits for A. Neither can finish, so neither will ever release what it holds. That is a deadlock: a cycle of transactions, each waiting for a lock the next one holds. Try it in the simulator: run A's first line, then B's.

PostgreSQL does not wait forever. A transaction that has waited for a lock for deadlock_timeout (1 second by default) checks the graph of who waits for whom. If it finds a cycle, it aborts one transaction with SQLSTATE 40P01, deadlock detected, and a DETAIL that names both processes. The other transaction gets its lock and finishes. Which one is aborted is hard to predict. The cost is a second of waiting and a transaction to retry: lesson 12's retry loop already treats 40P01 like 40001.

The fix is to make the cycle impossible: every transaction takes its locks in the same order. Sort the two account ids and lock the lower one first, whichever way the money moves:

SELECT account_id FROM accounts
WHERE account_id IN (109, 209)
ORDER BY account_id
FOR UPDATE;              -- both transfers lock 109, then 209

Now B's first lock request is for 109, which A holds, so B waits while holding nothing, and A finishes. The same rule covers a Kafka consumer that applies a batch of balance changes one row at a time. Two consumers whose batches touch the same accounts in different orders will deadlock now and then; sorting each batch first makes every consumer lock in the same order:

for (change in batch.sortedBy { it.accountId }) {     // every consumer locks in ascending id order
    update.setLong(1, change.amountMinor)
    update.setLong(2, change.accountId)
    update.executeUpdate()                            // holds this row's lock until COMMIT
}
conn.commit()

Two more tools belong here. SET lock_timeout = '2s' makes any statement that waits longer for a lock fail with 55P03, so a stuck holder cannot hang a request; a wait without a deadlock lasts forever otherwise. And when what you need to serialize is not a row, use an advisory lock, a lock on a number your application picks. SELECT pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(1, 20260612) returns true for the first pod that wants to settle merchant 1's day and false for every other, and PostgreSQL releases it at COMMIT. Prefer the _xact_ functions with a connection pool: the session-level pg_advisory_lock survives COMMIT and stays with the pooled connection after your code has closed it.

sim.title: Two transfers between 109 and 209
sim.intro: Each UPDATE first takes its row's lock, then reads, changes and writes the balance. Run A to the end, then B: both finish. Reset, then run A's first line and B's first line, and keep going.

goal.say: Both transfers committed: 109 holds 7,000 and 209 holds 3,000. One transfer ran while the other waited at its first lock. Reset, run A's first line, then B's first line: each holds one row and needs the other's. PostgreSQL would abort one of them after a second, with 40P01.

try.title: Make a deadlock, then prevent it
steps: Open two terminals in the labs folder and run psql in both: docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz -d course. Call them A and B. Turn on \timing on in both. Start the database if it is not running (docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait, from the labs folder).

Run the first block, switching terminals at each comment. After B's second UPDATE, wait. About a second later one terminal prints ERROR: deadlock detected. Usually it is the one that started waiting first, A. Run ROLLBACK in that terminal and COMMIT in the other, then read the balances.
Run the second block. Both transfers now start by locking the two accounts in id order. Does anything wait, and does anything fail?

code.title: psql, two sessions on database course
code.html: -- 1. A moves 1,000 from 109 to 209; B moves 3,000 from 209 to 109 -- A BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance_minor = balance_minor - 1000 WHERE account_id = 109; -- B BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance_minor = balance_minor - 3000 WHERE account_id = 209; -- A (waits for B) UPDATE accounts SET balance_minor = balance_minor + 1000 WHERE account_id = 209; -- B (waits for A: a cycle) UPDATE accounts SET balance_minor = balance_minor + 3000 WHERE account_id = 109; -- the terminal with the error: ROLLBACK; the other: COMMIT SELECT account_id, balance_minor FROM accounts WHERE account_id IN (109, 209) ORDER BY account_id; UPDATE accounts SET balance_minor = 5000 WHERE account_id IN (109, 209); -- 2. the same transfers, locking in account_id order first -- A BEGIN; SELECT account_id FROM accounts WHERE account_id IN (109, 209) ORDER BY account_id FOR UPDATE; -- B (waits for A, holding nothing) BEGIN; SELECT account_id FROM accounts WHERE account_id IN (209, 109) ORDER BY account_id FOR UPDATE; -- A UPDATE accounts SET balance_minor = balance_minor - 1000 WHERE account_id = 109; UPDATE accounts SET balance_minor = balance_minor + 1000 WHERE account_id = 209; COMMIT; -- B UPDATE accounts SET balance_minor = balance_minor - 3000 WHERE account_id = 209; UPDATE accounts SET balance_minor = balance_minor + 3000 WHERE account_id = 109; COMMIT; SELECT account_id, balance_minor FROM accounts WHERE account_id IN (109, 209) ORDER BY account_id; UPDATE accounts SET balance_minor = 5000 WHERE account_id IN (109, 209);

try.expect:
In block 1, one second after B's second UPDATE starts waiting (here it was A that lost; your process and transaction numbers differ):

ERROR:  deadlock detected
DETAIL:  Process 6685 waits for ShareLock on transaction 6950; blocked by process 6699.
Process 6699 waits for ShareLock on transaction 6949; blocked by process 6685.
HINT:  See server log for query details.
CONTEXT:  while updating tuple (0,49) in relation "accounts"
Time: 1006.392 ms (00:01.006)

\echo :SQLSTATE there prints 40P01. At the same instant the other terminal's UPDATE finishes. After the ROLLBACK and the COMMIT only B's transfer happened: 109 is 8000 and 209 is 2000 (if B got the error instead, you see A's transfer: 4000 and 6000). The aborted transfer must be retried. In block 2, B's locking SELECT waits about as long as A takes, then returns both ids, and nothing fails. The final SELECT shows 109 at 7000 and 209 at 3000: both transfers, applied once each. Each block ends by putting 5,000 back.

analogy: Picture a warehouse where pickers fill orders from one shelf of parcels, oldest first. A row lock is a reserved tag a picker hangs on a parcel. With FOR UPDATE, a picker who reaches a tagged parcel stands and waits for the tag to come off, even though the next parcel is free. SKIP LOCKED walks past tagged parcels to the first free one. NOWAIT turns around and reports back. A deadlock is two pickers who each hold one parcel and wait for the other's; the fixed-order rule is "always take the lower shelf number first". The analogy breaks in two places. In PostgreSQL, anyone may still look at a tagged parcel: a plain SELECT reads the last committed version and never waits. And a tag disappears the moment its transaction ends, including when the picker's pod is killed, because the server rolls back a transaction whose connection is gone.
world: The transactional outbox is this lesson in a payments service. The payment and an outbox row commit in one transaction; a relay claims outbox rows with ORDER BY id LIMIT 100 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, publishes them to Kafka and marks them sent, and you can run as many relay pods as you like. Kafka delivers at least once anyway, so consumers already need an idempotency key, the payment_uid of the course schema. A Quarkus @Scheduled settlement job runs on every pod; pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(merchant, day) lets exactly one of them settle each merchant's day. On Oracle at work, FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED exists too, but a deadlock (ORA-00060) rolls back only the statement that detected it, so your code must roll back the rest itself. And Temporal activities that move money between accounts should lock those accounts in id order, or two workflows moving money in opposite directions will deadlock and retry.
mistake: Building a job queue with a plain SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, or with a SELECT followed by an UPDATE, and keeping the transaction open for the whole job. People do it because it passes every test with one worker; the second worker only shows up in production under load. The SELECT-then-UPDATE version runs jobs twice: two receipts, two fraud reviews. The FOR UPDATE version runs each job once, but the workers queue behind each other, so ten pods drain the queue at the speed of one, and adding pods changes nothing. Add SKIP LOCKED to the claim, keep the claim to one statement that returns the job, decide whether the lock or a locked_at lease guards a running job, and make the job safe to run twice.

compare.title: Claiming a job and surviving a deadlock: Oracle and PostgreSQL

a.label: Oracle
a.title: Oracle AI Database 26ai
a.html: -- 26ai: FETCH FIRST with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED is new SELECT job_id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'queued' AND run_after <= SYSTIMESTAMP ORDER BY run_after, job_id FETCH FIRST 1 ROWS ONLY FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED; -- older code: open the cursor with no limit and fetch -- one row; WHERE ROWNUM = 1 ... SKIP LOCKED returns -- nothing when that one row is already locked -- FOR UPDATE WAIT 2 wait at most 2 seconds -- no FOR SHARE or FOR KEY SHARE: row locks are -- always exclusive -- deadlock: ORA-00060 rolls back the STATEMENT; -- the transaction is still open and still holds -- its other locks until you ROLLBACK

b.label: PostgreSQL 18
b.title: PostgreSQL 18
b.html: -- LIMIT with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED since 9.5 SELECT job_id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'queued' AND run_after <= now() ORDER BY run_after, job_id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED; -- locking stops once LIMIT has its row, so a locked -- first row is skipped and the next free one is -- returned -- no WAIT n: SET lock_timeout = '2s' (55P03) -- four modes: FOR UPDATE, FOR NO KEY UPDATE, -- FOR SHARE, FOR KEY SHARE (foreign-key checks) -- deadlock: 40P01 aborts the whole TRANSACTION; -- after it only ROLLBACK works, and every lock -- is released

compare.note: Both databases store row locks with the rows rather than in a memory table, and both have SKIP LOCKED for queues, so the claim looks almost the same. Three things differ in practice. Limiting the claim: PostgreSQL's LIMIT counts only the rows it managed to lock, while Oracle accepts FETCH FIRST together with FOR UPDATE only since 26ai, so older Oracle queue code fetches from an unbounded SKIP LOCKED cursor. Lock modes: Oracle has one exclusive row lock, and its foreign-key trap is a different one (an unindexed foreign key makes a parent DELETE lock the whole child table). Deadlocks: PostgreSQL aborts the whole transaction, Oracle rolls back one statement and leaves the transaction open, so Oracle code must roll back explicitly before it retries.

worked.title: A receipt worker in Kotlin: claim, commit, work, and a reaper

steps.say: Sending a receipt calls an email provider that can take seconds, so this worker uses claim and commit. The claim is its own short transaction: one statement, then COMMIT at once. Commit before the slow part and nothing stays locked while the email goes out.
steps.code: // 1. claim one job in a short transaction of its own data class Job(val id: Long, val payload: String, val attempts: Int) fun claim(conn: Connection, worker: String): Job? { conn.autoCommit = false val job = conn.prepareStatement( """ UPDATE jobs SET status = 'running', locked_by = ?, locked_at = now(), attempts = attempts + 1 WHERE job_id = (SELECT job_id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'queued' AND kind = 'send_receipt' AND run_after <= now() ORDER BY run_after, job_id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) RETURNING job_id, payload, attempts """, ).use { ps -> ps.setString(1, worker) ps.executeQuery().use { rs -> if (rs.next()) Job(rs.getLong(1), rs.getString(2), rs.getInt(3)) else null } } conn.commit() // the claim is visible to everyone, and no lock is held return job }

steps.say: The work runs outside any transaction. A second short transaction records the outcome. On failure the job goes back to the queue with a delay that grows with each attempt, and after the third attempt it stops at failed, like job 6 in the seed.
steps.code: // 2. do the work, then record the outcome in a second short transaction interface ReceiptMailer { fun send(payload: String, idempotencyKey: String) } fun runOne(conn: Connection, worker: String, mail: ReceiptMailer) { val job = claim(conn, worker) ?: return val ok = runCatching { mail.send(job.payload, idempotencyKey = "job-${job.id}") }.isSuccess conn.prepareStatement( """ UPDATE jobs SET status = CASE WHEN ? THEN 'done' WHEN attempts >= 3 THEN 'failed' ELSE 'queued' END, run_after = now() + attempts * interval '1 minute', locked_by = NULL, locked_at = NULL WHERE job_id = ? AND locked_by = ? """, ).use { ps -> ps.setBoolean(1, ok); ps.setLong(2, job.id); ps.setString(3, worker); ps.executeUpdate() } conn.commit() }

steps.say: A worker that dies between the claim and the outcome leaves its job running with an old locked_at. The reaper puts such jobs back. It is one UPDATE, so it is safe to run on every pod every minute: row locks make each job move once. The locked_by = ? in step 2 stops a slow worker from overwriting a job that the reaper already handed to someone else.
steps.code: -- 3. the reaper: put back jobs whose worker went quiet 10 minutes ago UPDATE jobs SET status = CASE WHEN attempts >= 3 THEN 'failed' ELSE 'queued' END, locked_by = NULL, locked_at = NULL WHERE status = 'running' AND locked_at < now() - interval '10 minutes';

steps.say: Claim and commit means a job can run twice: the worker sent the email, then died before step 2 committed, and the reaper queued it again. So the side effect carries a key that stays the same across attempts. The email provider drops a second request with the same key, the same way the payments table drops a second payment_uid (lesson 10).
steps.code: // 4. the same key on every attempt of one job: a repeat is harmless mail.send(job.payload, idempotencyKey = "job-${job.id}") // not a random UUID per attempt // with a lock-held design instead (BEGIN, claim, work, done, COMMIT), a crash rolls the claim // back and the job is simply queued again, but attempts rolls back too: it can't count crashes

lab.title: A job queue that never double-claims, and transfers that never deadlock
steps: With Docker running, run the tests from the labs folder. Six of the ten fail. The tests open real sessions at once (up to six workers) and commit for real, then put the seed back.

claim_job.sql is one statement that a worker runs inside its own open transaction. Read the failures: one says a worker waited for another worker's lock, one shows job 2 claimed twice with attempts = 2.
Fix the claim. Add a plain FOR UPDATE first and run the tests: the double claim goes away, and the waiting does not. Then make it skip what other workers hold.

transfer.sql moves money between the two accounts in a temp table transfer. Two sessions run it in opposite directions, one statement at a time. Read the log in the failure: it shows the deadlock and the retry. Make every transfer lock its two accounts in the same order before it changes them.
Run the tests until all ten pass. The last one checks that you lock only the two accounts: Ivy's transfer must not wait for Ben's.
hints: Put FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED at the end of the subquery, after LIMIT 1. The outer UPDATE then changes a row its own subquery already holds.

For the transfer, add one statement after BEGIN: SELECT a.account_id FROM accounts a, transfer t WHERE a.account_id IN (t.from_account, t.to_account) ORDER BY a.account_id FOR UPDATE OF a;. OF a locks only the account rows.
LOCK TABLE accounts also stops the deadlock, and fails the last test: every transfer in the company would wait for every other one.

drill.title: The claim and the lock order, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write (1) the statement a worker runs to claim the oldest due queued job from jobs, mark it running and return it, so that ten workers at once never wait for each other and never get the same job; and (2) the first statement of a transfer between accounts :from and :to that makes deadlocks between transfers impossible. Then say which lock mode a foreign-key check takes on the parent row.

answer.html: -- 1. the claim UPDATE jobs SET status = 'running', locked_by = :worker, locked_at = now(), attempts = attempts + 1 WHERE job_id = (SELECT job_id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'queued' AND run_after <= now() ORDER BY run_after, job_id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) RETURNING job_id, kind, payload; -- 2. lock both accounts, lowest id first, before changing either SELECT account_id FROM accounts WHERE account_id IN (:from, :to) ORDER BY account_id FOR UPDATE; -- 3. FOR KEY SHARE: it conflicts only with FOR UPDATE (a DELETE, a key change, -- or an explicit SELECT ... FOR UPDATE), not with an ordinary UPDATE

recap: A row lock is a mark a transaction writes into the row version it locks; it lasts until COMMIT or ROLLBACK. Writers and lockers wait for it, plain readers never do. A waiter sleeps on the holder's transaction id.

Read-then-update claims run a job twice. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE fixes that but makes workers queue behind the first row. FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED lets each worker take the next row nobody holds; NOWAIT fails at once with 55P03.
Hold the claim's transaction open only for short jobs: the lock is then a lease that a crash releases. For slow jobs, claim and commit, track locked_at, run a reaper, and make the work idempotent.

Row lock modes, strongest first: FOR UPDATE (DELETE, key change), FOR NO KEY UPDATE (any other UPDATE), FOR SHARE, FOR KEY SHARE (foreign-key checks). Lock a parent you will only update with FOR NO KEY UPDATE, or its children's inserts wait.
A deadlock is a cycle of lock waits. PostgreSQL breaks it after deadlock_timeout (1 s) by aborting one transaction with 40P01. Prevent it by locking rows in a fixed order, such as ascending id.
lock_timeout bounds every lock wait. Advisory locks serialize things that are not rows; use the _xact_ functions with a pool.

explain.prompt: A teammate wants to process payout jobs from a PostgreSQL table with ten pods, each running SELECT * FROM payouts_queue WHERE status = 'new' ORDER BY id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE, then calling the bank, then marking the row done, all in one transaction. Explain what will happen under load and what you would change.
explain.answer: Every pod picks the same oldest row from the same snapshot, so one pod gets its lock and nine wait for it. The first pod holds the lock for the whole bank call, maybe a second, so the nine sit idle and then collide again on the next row. No payout runs twice, which is why tests pass, but ten pods drain the queue at the speed of one, and adding pods only adds waiters. I'd add SKIP LOCKED so each pod takes the oldest row nobody holds, and fold the claim into one UPDATE ... WHERE id = (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) RETURNING. Because a bank call is slow, I would not hold the transaction open across it: commit the claim with a locked_at time, call the bank, and mark the row done in a second short transaction. That needs a reaper for rows stuck in running and an idempotency key on the bank call that stays the same across attempts, because a reaped payout may already have been sent. I'd also check there is a partial index on the queue's ordering column for status = 'new', so a claim stays a few pages as done rows accumulate.

deeper.html:
When several transactions lock one row at once, as the foreign-key checks of many payments on one card do, a single transaction id no longer fits in the row header. PostgreSQL then writes a MultiXact id there instead: a pointer to a list of lockers and their modes, kept in pg_multixact. That is the multi = t in the pgrowlocks output. MultiXact ids wrap around like transaction ids, and a very busy parent row can make that storage grow, which is one reason to keep foreign-key parents that every insert touches (a single "platform merchant" row, say) out of hot paths.

SKIP LOCKED gives a deliberately inconsistent view. The PostgreSQL docs say it is unsuitable for general work but suits "multiple consumers accessing a queue-like table". Never use it for a report or a balance check: a row you skipped still exists.

Polling an empty queue every 100 ms from ten pods is cheap with the partial index, but LISTEN and NOTIFY can wake workers instead. A trigger or the inserting code runs NOTIFY jobs_ready, each idle worker holds a connection in LISTEN jobs_ready, and pgJDBC delivers the notification through PGConnection.getNotifications(). Keep the polling as a fallback: a notification sent while a worker is restarting is lost.

A queue table is an UPDATE-heavy table, and every UPDATE in PostgreSQL writes a new row version (lesson 12's MVCC). Delete or archive done jobs in batches, or partition the table by day and drop old partitions, and let autovacuum visit it more often than the default, which waits until 20% of a table's rows are dead (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.2; set it lower on this one table).

At REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on a row that another transaction changed and committed after your snapshot fails with 40001 instead of returning the new version. Queue claims belong at Read Committed, where the recheck you saw in the first Try it moves the worker on to the next row.

The engine side is in the database internals track, "Concurrency control: locks, deadlocks and SSI": the lock manager's tables, the wait-for graph and the cycle search behind 40P01.
